results.title: Omnigraph: a graph database designed for agents · Modern Relay
results.content:
## Branches

Agents write too, constantly and in bulk, so writes have to be safe. In Omnigraph every agent gets its own branch and works in isolation. Useful work merges, slop is discarded. Autonomous writes become proposals you review rather than raw changes to live data.

The real unlock is that branches let agents make mistakes. A long-running agent enriching thousands of nodes will get some of them wrong: a bad merge, a mislabeled edge, an enum in the wrong place. On a branch the mess stays on the branch, and the main graph never sees it.

[figure 04]

Two agents, two branches. Hermes's ingest passes review and merges. Claude's enrichment run mislabels an edge; review catches it and the branch is thrown away. Main never saw either until one of them was reviewed. [...] We think that rather than patch the old model, it's time to ask what a database looks like when its user is an agent. The hard and interesting part is figuring out the right primitives: the scoped units of a write or a deployment, where a boundary belongs, where correctness has to win over speed, and many more.

We don't think we have all of it right. We get feedback every day, and we make it better.

If you use Omnigraph, please don't hesitate to tell us what works and what breaks.

← All posts [...] And whose is it? As open-source models get better, AI sovereignty becomes a real deployment target rather than a preference. The graph is the organisation's memory; a corrupted one or a locked-in one is the failure. Branches guard against the first. Ownership guards against the second, and it cannot be conditional. An export button is not ownership: it means you fully control the data and the definition. Omnigraph is built on the open Lance format, fully open source, with no vendor lock-in.

## Wrapping up

Legacy databases were shaped by a world of human-scale throughput, stable schemas, slow operators, and clear scenarios (OLTP or OLAP). That world is gone.

results.content:
### What database should I use for AI agent memory?

+

One your agents can write to safely and you can audit. In Omnigraph each agent writes on its own branch, the schema is enforced on every write, Cedar policies run inside the engine, and changes reach main only through a merge you can diff first. Every version stays readable, so you can see what an agent knew and when.

### Is Omnigraph a Neo4j alternative?

+

For agent workloads, yes. Neo4j is a mature graph database. Omnigraph is MIT-licensed, keeps the graph as open files in storage you own, and is built around what agents need: git-style branches and merges, a typed schema checked on every write, built-in vector and full-text search, and in-engine policy.

## FAQ

### What is a context graph?

+

A graph of what your agents need to know: people, projects, decisions, documents, and how they connect, kept current as agents and people work. Omnigraph is the database underneath one: typed, versioned, and searchable by graph traversal, vector and full-text in a single query.

### Is Omnigraph an open source graph database?

+

Yes. The engine, CLI and server are MIT-licensed on GitHub. The graph is stored as open Lance files in S3-compatible storage, Azure Blob (in preview) or a local directory, so it runs anywhere: embedded on a laptop with no server, or in your own cloud account.
